source: the two groups (purple and pink curves) had identical average signal envelopes (Figure 5A), but displayed significantly disparate EEG responses (Figure 5B), with significantly larger responses to the notes with the high pitch surprise (purple >pink; p<0.05 at the N1 and P2 peaks, permutation test; p=0.001 on the power of the average ERP across all channels for latencies between 0 and 200 ms).

source: and high-γ ECoG data (r = 0.88, p=0.002 for e6 in the left TTS of Patient 1; r = 0.88, p=0.002 for e9 in the left HG of Patient 1; Figure 6D).
evidence: Statistical test results reported in the results section with specific correlation values and p-values.

claim: A cluster statistics indicated that melodic expectation was larger for musicians than non-musicians for frontal EEG channels.
source: A cluster statistics indicated that melodic expectation was larger for musicians than non-musicians for frontal EEG channels (Figure 7B

claim: Subjective reporting indicated no significant effect of musical training on the familiarity with the musical pieces.
source: Note that subjective reporting indicated no significant effect of musical training on the familiarity with the musical pieces (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Direct statement about behavioral results in the results section.

claim: Humans engagement in music rests on underlying elements such as the listeners' cultural background and interest in music.
source: Humans engagement in music rests on underlying elements such as the listeners' cultural background and interest in music.
evidence: Statement in the abstract drawing on established understanding of music perception.

claim: These factors modulate how listeners anticipate musical events, a process inducing instantaneous neural responses as the music confronts these expectations.
source: These factors modulate how listeners anticipate musical events, a process inducing instantaneous neural responses as the music confronts these expectations.
evidence: Statement in the abstract drawing on established understanding of predictive processing.

claim: This encoding was most pronounced at response latencies up to 350 ms, and in both planum temporale and Heschl's gyrus.
source: This encoding was most pronounced at response latencies up to 350 ms, and in both planum temporale and Heschl's gyrus.
evidence: Summary statement in the abstract based on the study's findings.

claim: Through active auditory engagement, humans analyze and comprehend complex musical scenes by invoking the cultural norms of music, segregating sound mixtures, and marshaling expectations and anticipation.
source: Through this active auditory engagement, humans analyze and comprehend complex musical scenes by invoking the cultural norms of music, segregating sound mixtures, and marshaling expectations and anticipation (Huron, 2006).
evidence: Statement in the introduction supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Structural knowledge that listeners acquire and encode through frequent exposure to music is thought to shape listeners' expectations and to determine what constitutes a 'familiar' musical style.
source: Ultimately, this knowledge is thought to shape listeners' expectations and to determine what constitutes a 'familiar' musical style that they are likely to understand and appreciate (Morrison et al., 2008; Hannon et al., 2012; Pearce, 2018).
evidence: Statement in the introduction supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There is convincing evidence that musical structures can be learnt through the passive exposure of music in everyday life.
source: There is convincing evidence that musical structures can be learnt through the passive exposure of music in everyday life (Bigand and Poulin-Charronnat, 2006; Rohrmeier et al., 2011)
evidence: Statement in the introduction supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The connectionist model from Tillman and colleagues, which simulated implicit learning of pitch structures occurring in Western music, was shown to successfully predict behavioral and neurophysiological results on music perception.
source: The connectionist model from Tillman and colleagues, which simulated implicit learning of pitch structures occurring in Western music, was shown to successfully predict behavioral and neurophysiological results on music perception (Tillmann et al., 2000).
evidence: Statement in the introduction supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Failed predictions due to deviations in the sensory sequence produce measurable brain activations that have been associated with the detection and strength of these irregularities, that is prediction error.
source: Supporting evidence is that failed predictions due to deviations in the sensory sequence produce measurable brain activations that have been associated with the detection and strength of these irregularities, that is prediction error (Vuust et al., 2012; Clark, 2013; Moldwin et al., 2017; Omigie et al., 2019; Quiroga-Martinez et al., 2019b; Quiroga-Martinez et al., 2019a)
evidence: Statement in the introduction supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Listeners have strong and well-defined musical expectations which depend on a person's musical culture.
source: Decades of research have established that listeners have strong and well-defined musical expectations (Schmuckler, 1989; Cuddy and Lunney, 1995; Margulis, 2005; Morgan et al., 2019) which depend on a person's musical culture (Carlsen, 1981; Kessler et al., 1984; Krumhansl et al., 2000; Eerola et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement in the introduction supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Violation of music expectations elicits consistent event-related potentials (ERPs), such as the mismatch negativity (MMN) or the early right-anterior negativity (ERAN), which typically emerges between 100 and 250 ms after the onset of the violation.
source: Neurophysiology studies demonstrated that violation of music expectations elicits consistent event-related potentials (ERPs), such as the mismatch negativity (MMN) or the early right-anterior negativity (ERAN), which typically emerges between 100 and 250 ms after the onset of the violation (Koelsch, 2009; Vuust et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement in the introduction supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Brain responses to violations of auditory regularities have been measured for a range of violations including out-of-key notes embedded in chords, unlikely chords, and single tones.
source: Such brain responses have been measured for a range of violations of auditory regularities, including out-of-key notes embedded in chords (e.g. Neapolitan sixth in Koelsch et al., 2000), unlikely chords (e.g. double dominant in Koelsch et al., 2007), and single tones (Miranda and Ullman, 2007; Omigie et al., 2013; Omigie et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement in the introduction supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ERP studies often limit the range of expectations' violations strength that are tested to severe violations because of the need for repeated stimulus presentations.
source: ERP studies (Besson and Macar, 1987; Paller et al., 1992; Miranda and Ullman, 2007; Pearce et al., 2010b; Carrus et al., 2013) often limit the range of expectations' violations strength that are tested to severe violations because of the need for repeated stimulus presentations.
evidence: Statement in the introduction about methodological limitations of prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Music sequences induce a wide range of violation strengths because the (valid) sequential events are not all equally likely.
source: In fact, music sequences induce a wide range of violation strengths (Pearce and Wiggins, 2012) because the (valid) sequential events are not all equally likely (and hence not equally predictable), whether we consider note or chord sequences (Temperley, 2008) in both classical music (Rohrmeier and Cross, 2008) or more popular music genres (Temperley and Clercq, 2013).
evidence: Statement in the introduction supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Melodies are a key structural aspect of music across musical styles and cultures.
source: One layer concerns the notes sequences forming melodies, which is a key structural aspect of music across musical styles (Reck, 1997) and cultures (Eerola, 2003; Pearce and Wiggins, 2006).
evidence: Statement in the introduction supported by citations to prior work.

claim: IDyOM attempts to optimally predict the next note in a melodic sequence by combining predictions based on long-term statistics learnt from a large corpus of western music and short-term statistics from the previous notes of the current musical stream.
source: This framework attempts to optimally predict the next note in a melodic sequence by combining predictions based on 1) long-term statistics learnt from a large corpus of western music and 2) short-term statistics from the previous notes of the current musical stream.
evidence: Statement in the introduction describing the IDyOM model based on prior work.

claim: IDyOM provides likelihood values for each note in a melody that have been shown to tightly mirror listeners' expectations.
source: In turn, this provides us with likelihood values for each note in a melody that have been shown to tightly mirror listeners' expectations (Pearce, 2005).
evidence: Statement in the introduction supported by citation to prior work.

claim: According to the predictive coding theory, cortical signals partly reflect the mismatch between a participant's prediction and the actual sensory input.
source: According to the predictive coding theory (Friston and Kiebel, 2009; Clark, 2013), cortical signals partly reflect the mismatch between a participant's prediction and the actual sensory input.
evidence: Statement in the introduction supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: If predictive coding theory is correct, less expected musical notes should produce relatively stronger cortical responses.
source: If this is the case, less expected musical notes should produce relatively stronger cortical responses.
evidence: Logical inference from predictive coding theory stated in the introduction.

claim: Individuals with musical expertise are expected to internally generate predictions on a next note that more closely relate the ones of a specialized statistical model than non-musicians.
source: We expected individuals with musical expertise to internally generate predictions on a next note that more closely relate the ones of a specialized statistical model than non-musicians.
evidence: Hypothesis stated in the introduction based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: Musical streams are imbued with melodic events that routinely violates listeners' expectation to some degree.
source: Musical streams are imbued with melodic events that routinely violates listeners' expectation to some degree (Pearce and Wiggins, 2012; Salimpoor et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement in the introduction supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The combination of both the acoustic and surprise features is expected to predict the neural responses better than either set of features alone.
source: we consequently expected the combination of both the acoustic and surprise features to predict the neural responses better than either set of features alone (Figure 1C).
evidence: Hypothesis stated in the introduction based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: This work presents novel insights into the precise spatio-temporal dynamics of the integration of melodic expectations and sensory input during naturalistic musical listening.
source: This work presents novel insights into the precise spatio-temporal dynamics of the integration of melodic expectations and sensory input during naturalistic musical listening.
evidence: Summary statement in the introduction about the study's contributions.

claim: The results provide evidence of the neurophysiological validity of predictive statistical models of music structure.
source: In turn, our results provide evidence of the neurophysiological validity of predictive statistical models of music structure.
evidence: Summary statement in the introduction about the study's contributions.

claim: Distinct encoding of different melodic expectation features (such as pitch and note onset) to the cortical responses to music was found.
source: Crucially, we found distinct encoding of different melodic expectation features, (such as pitch and note onset) to the cortical responses to music.
evidence: Summary statement in the introduction about the study's findings.

claim: Neural responses are consistent with the statistical learning theoretical frameworks in that response dynamics are proportional to the predictability of several signal attributes, including pitch and onset-timing.
source: First, we show that the neural responses are consistent with the statistical learning theoretical frameworks in that response dynamics are proportional to the predictability of several signal attributes, including pitch and onset-timing.
evidence: Summary statement in the discussion about the study's findings and their implications.

claim: Melodic expectations attributes are encoded in both low-rate and high-γ responses of higher cortical regions (e.g., bilateral PT in humans).
source: Second, melodic expectations attributes are encoded in both low-rate and high-γ responses of higher cortical regions (e.g., bilateral PT in humans).
evidence: Summary statement in the discussion about the study's findings.

claim: The effect of expectations extended to the junction between the PT with HG (TTS) and to neighbouring electrodes in HG.
source: The effect of expectations extended to the junction between the PT with HG (TTS) and to neighbouring electrodes in HG, an early auditory cortical area that favors the accurate representation of the acoustic properties of the music.
evidence: Summary statement in the discussion about the study's findings.

claim: Neural signals in some SMG electrodes showed similar encoding of melodic entropy and surprise, which aligns with previous findings suggesting a role of the left SMG in short-term pitch memory.
source: In addition, neural signals in some SMG electrodes showed similar encoding of melodic entropy and surprise, a result that well aligns with previous findings suggesting a role of the left SMG in short-term pitch memory (Vines et al., 2006; Schaal et al., 2015; Schaal et al., 2017).
evidence: Summary statement in the discussion about the study's findings, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A methodology was demonstrated to objectively assess the cortical encoding of melodic expectations using non-invasive neural recordings and passive listening of ecologically valid stimuli.
source: Third, we have demonstrated a methodology to objectively assess the cortical encoding of melodic expectations using non-invasive neural recordings and passive listening of ecologically valid stimuli.
evidence: Summary statement in the discussion about the study's methodological contributions.

claim: The TRF framework is more resistant to the issue of isolating responses to continuous or rapidly presented stimuli than the ERP approach.
source: Instead, the TRF framework is more resistant to this issue as it assumes that the transformation of a stimulus into the corresponding brain responses can be captured by a linear time-invariant system.
evidence: Statement in the discussion about methodological advantages based on theoretical understanding.

claim: The TRF approach was shown to be effective in previous studies with stimuli that were either discrete and rapidly presented, or continuous.
source: Although the human brain is neither linear nor time-invariant, these assumptions can be reasonable in certain cases, and this approach was shown to be effective in previous studies with stimuli that were either discrete and rapidly presented, or continuous (Lalor et al., 2006; Ding and Simon, 2012b; Di Liberto et al., 2015; Crosse et al., 2016; Fiedler et al., 2017; Brodbeck et al., 2018a; Broderick et al., 2018; Vanthornhout et al., 2018; Wong et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement in the discussion supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Information on melodic expectations, as well as levels and fidelity of envelope tracking, can be extracted from both EEG and ECoG recordings using the TRF approach.
source: Using this approach, we have demonstrated how information on melodic expectations, as well as levels and fidelity of envelope tracking, can be extracted from both EEG and ECoG recordings.
evidence: Summary statement in the discussion about the study's findings.

claim: Melodic expectations of various origins modulate responses to stimulus acoustics, possibly increasing the magnitude of those responses according to the degree of violation of the expectations.
source: There is ample evidence that melodic expectations of various origins modulate responses to stimulus acoustics, possibly increasing the magnitude of those responses according to the degree of violation of the expectations.
evidence: Statement in the discussion drawing on established understanding and the study's findings.

claim: The positive expectation component at latencies between 150 and 250 ms corresponds to the same latencies as ERP components elicited by musical violations such as the ERAN.
source: Such a modulation was captured by our multivariate TRF analysis in Figure 2E, which emerged as a positive expectation component at latencies between 150 and 250 ms, the same latencies corresponding to ERP components elicited by musical violations such as the ERAN (Koelsch et al., 2002).
evidence: Statement in the discussion comparing the study's findings to prior work, supported by citation.

claim: Musical expertise may significantly enhance the modulations of musical responses by expectations and hence reveal stronger encoding of melodic expectations.
source: Furthermore, since subjects' expectations modulate musical responses differently depending on their cultural experience and musical exposure, it is expected that musical expertise may significantly enhance these modulations and hence reveal stronger encoding of melodic expectations.
evidence: Statement in the discussion based on theoretical reasoning and the study's findings.

claim: The evidence on musical expertise is consistent with previous neuroimaging results showing effects of musical training on the brain responses to music in both children and adults.
source: The evidence we present in this study (Figure 7) is in line with this view and, although preliminary, the finding is consistent with previous neuroimaging results showing effects of musical training on the brain responses to music in both children and adults (e.g. Jentschke and Koelsch, 2009; Oechslin et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement in the discussion comparing the study's findings to prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Rich predictive models can be combined with neural recordings to disentangle the processing of distinct properties of complex sensory inputs.
source: The present study demonstrates that rich predictive models can be combined with neural recordings to disentangle the processing of distinct properties of complex sensory inputs.
evidence: Summary statement in the discussion about the study's methodological contributions.

claim: Previous work demonstrated that combining predictive models with neural recordings is effective in other domains, such as in the study of natural speech perception.
source: Previous work demonstrated that this approach is effective in other domains, such as in the study of natural speech perception, where neural responses at the level of acoustics, phonemes, phonotactics, and semantics were measured (Di Liberto et al., 2015; Di Liberto et al., 2019; Brodbeck et al., 2018c; Broderick et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement in the discussion supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The hypothesis of shared resources between language and music has been supported by evidence of overlapping brain responses for processing music and language structures.
source: For instance, the hypothesis of shared resources between language and music has been supported by evidence of overlapping brain responses for processing music and language structures (Maess et al., 2001).
evidence: Statement in the discussion supported by citation to prior work.

claim: It is unclear whether overlapping brain responses for music and language reflect domain-specific computations or domain-general functions such as working memory or cognitive control.
source: However, it is unclear whether these effects reflect domain-specific computations or domain-general functions such as working memory or cognitive control (Rogalsky et al., 2011; Fitch and Martins, 2014)
evidence: Statement in the discussion supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In speech, expectations are important to successfully understand the meaning of a sentence, especially in noisy, multi-talker environments.
source: In speech, expectations are important to successfully understand the meaning of a sentence (e.g., phonemic restoration, priming; Leonard et al., 2016; Norris et al., 2016), especially in noisy, multi-talker environments (McGettigan et al., 2012; Strauß et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement in the discussion supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In music, expectations may have a stronger link to emotions and musical engagement.
source: In music, expectations may have a stronger link to emotions and musical engagement (Dunsby, 2014; Salimpoor et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement in the discussion supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The results on melodic expectations exhibited spatio-temporal patterns that are different from those for the typical ERPs for syntactic and semantic violations in the case of natural speech perception (N400, P600).
source: Our results on melodic expectations exhibited spatio-temporal patterns that are different from those for the typical ERPs for syntactic and semantic violations in the case of natural speech perception, (N400, P600; for example Osterhout and Holcomb, 1995; Kutas and Federmeier, 2011; Borovsky et al., 2012).
